events.title: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt
events.description: Pharaoh Menes (Narmer) unified Upper and Lower Egypt, establishing the First Dynasty and beginning 3000 years of Egyptian civilization. Menes founded Memphis as capital, establishing divine pharaonic rule. This marked birth of one of world's earliest unified states, with Egyptian hieroglyphic writing system developing during this period.

events.title: Old Kingdom Period (Pyramid Age)
events.description: Egyptian Old Kingdom period, Third to Sixth Dynasties rule. This was golden age of pyramid construction, with Giza pyramid complex built including Great Pyramid of Khufu (one of Seven Wonders of Ancient World). Pharaonic power reached zenith, centralized government perfected. Art, architecture, medicine and astronomy flourished. Egypt called 'Land of Pyramid Builders' during this era.

events.title: Sneferu's Pyramid Construction
events.description: Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Sneferu built three pyramids: Meidum Pyramid, Bent Pyramid, and Red Pyramid. These architectural experiments laid technical foundation for later perfect Giza pyramids. Sneferu's architectural achievements marked Egypt's transition from step pyramids to true pyramids, demonstrating rapid development of ancient Egyptian engineering technology.

events.title: Completion of Great Pyramid of Khufu
events.description: Great Pyramid built by pharaoh Khufu (Fourth Dynasty) completed, standing 146.5 meters tall, tallest building in ancient world. This pyramid employed approximately 100,000 workers, took 20 years to complete, using 2.3 million limestone blocks. Great Pyramid of Khufu remains only surviving structure of Seven Wonders of Ancient World, showcasing ancient Egyptian civilization's architectural marvel and organizational capacity.

events.title: Middle Kingdom Period
events.description: Prosperity period after Eleventh Dynasty reunified Egypt. Capital moved to Thebes, literature and art reached new heights. Egypt expanded south to Nubia, controlling gold trade. Social system improved, important texts like Book of the Dead appeared. Middle Kingdom considered classical period of Egyptian culture.

events.title: Hyksos Rule
events.description: Asian Hyksos people conquered Lower Egypt, introducing new technologies like horses, chariots and bronze weapons. Though viewed as 'foreign rule,' Hyksos adopted Egyptian culture, promoting technological exchange. This period stimulated Egyptian military innovation, laying foundation for later New Kingdom expansion.

events.title: New Kingdom Period (Imperial Age)
events.description: Most glorious period in Egyptian history, Eighteenth to Twentieth Dynasties rule. Egypt became superpower of eastern Mediterranean, territory extending from Nubia to Euphrates River. Famous pharaohs included Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II. Great buildings like Abu Simbel temples constructed.

events.title: Akhenaten's Religious Revolution
events.description: Pharaoh Akhenaten (originally Amenhotep IV) promoted monotheistic reform worshipping sun god Aten, establishing new capital Amarna. This was one of earliest monotheistic attempts in human history. Reform caused strong opposition from priest class, abandoned after Akhenaten's death, but profoundly influenced later religious thought.

events.title: Reign of Ramesses II
events.description: Ramesses II (Ramesses the Great) ruled 67 years, one of longest-reigning pharaohs in Egyptian history. He signed first peace treaty in human history with Hittite Empire, built magnificent structures like Abu Simbel temples. Ramesses II possibly the pharaoh who opposed Moses in Bible, his reign marked last glory of Egyptian Empire.

events.title: Battle of Kadesh
events.description: Ramesses II led Egyptian army in major battle against Hittite Empire at Kadesh in Syria. This was one of largest chariot battles in ancient history, with both sides deploying thousands of chariots. Though both claimed victory, actual result was inconclusive. This battle ultimately led to Egypt and Hittites signing first international peace treaty in human history, pioneering diplomatic negotiation for conflict resolution.

events.title: Late Period
events.description: Egypt entered decline, successively ruled by Libyans, Nubians, Assyrians, Persians. Twenty-fifth Dynasty Nubian pharaohs briefly revived Egypt. Persian Achaemenid Empire twice conquered Egypt (525 BCE and 343 BCE), Egypt became Persian province. Despite political turmoil, Egyptian cultural traditions maintained.

events.title: Alexander the Great's Conquest
events.description: Macedonian King Alexander the Great conquered Egypt, ending Persian rule. Alexander viewed as liberator by Egyptians, he respected Egyptian religious traditions, crowned as pharaoh. Alexander founded Alexandria in Nile Delta, city later became most important cultural and commercial center in Mediterranean.

events.title: Ptolemaic Dynasty
events.description: After Alexander's death, his general Ptolemy I established Ptolemaic Dynasty, ruling Egypt nearly 300 years. Alexandria became cultural center of Hellenistic world, housing famous Library of Alexandria and Lighthouse (one of Seven Wonders). Ptolemaic Dynasty adopted pharaonic traditions but introduced Greek culture, creating unique Greco-Egyptian civilization fusion.

events.title: Cleopatra VII's Reign
events.description: Last pharaoh of Ptolemaic Dynasty Cleopatra VII, famous for beauty, intelligence and political acumen. She successively allied with Caesar and Mark Antony, attempting to maintain Egyptian independence. Cleopatra was first Ptolemaic ruler to learn Egyptian language, beloved by people. Her death marked end of ancient Egyptian civilization.

events.title: Roman Conquest
events.description: Octavian (later Augustus) defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Battle of Actium, Egypt became Roman province. Egypt became Rome's granary, annually providing large amounts of wheat to Rome. Under Roman rule, Egypt economically prosperous but politically declined, ancient Egyptian religion gradually declined.

events.title: Introduction of Christianity
events.description: Christianity introduced to Egypt during Roman rule, tradition says Apostle Mark established church in Alexandria. Egypt became important early Christian center, developing distinctive Coptic Christianity. Monasticism arose in Egypt, Saint Anthony hailed as father of monasticism. Alexandria's theological school became Christian academic center.

events.title: Diocletian Persecution
events.description: Roman Emperor Diocletian launched last major persecution of Christians, Egyptian Christians suffered severe persecution. Many Christians martyred, churches destroyed. This period called 'Era of Martyrs' by Coptic Church. Despite persecution, Christianity continued growing in Egypt.

events.title: Constantine's Edict of Toleration
events.description: Roman Emperor Constantine issued Edict of Milan, Christianity gained legal status in Egypt. Egyptian Christianity rapidly developed, churches built extensively. Alexandria's Patriarch became important leader of Eastern Christianity. Egypt played important role in early Christian theological development.

events.title: Council of Nicaea
events.description: First Council of Nicaea convened, Egyptian Alexandria Patriarch Athanasius played key role in opposing Arianism. Council established Trinity doctrine, profoundly influencing Christian development. Egyptian Church played important role in forming early Christian orthodox doctrine.

events.title: Division of Roman Empire
events.description: Roman Empire formally divided into East and West, Egypt belonged to Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine Empire). Constantinople became new political center, but Egypt maintained important economic position. Under Byzantine rule, Egyptian Christian culture further developed, but theological differences with Constantinople gradually deepened.

events.title: Council of Chalcedon Split
events.description: After Council of Chalcedon, Egyptian Coptic Church split from Byzantine Orthodox Church for refusing to accept Christ's two natures doctrine. Coptic Church insisted on Monophysitism, becoming independent Oriental Orthodox Church. This theological difference deepened political opposition between Egypt and Byzantine Empire, laying groundwork for later Arab conquest.

events.title: Persian Sassanid Conquest
events.description: Persian Sassanid Empire briefly occupied Egypt during Byzantine-Persian Wars. Though Persian rule was brief, it further weakened Byzantine rule foundation in Egypt. War damaged Egyptian economy, people's dissatisfaction with Byzantine rule intensified. This created favorable conditions for Arab conquest.

events.title: Arab Conquest of Egypt
events.description: Arab general Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt, ending Byzantine rule. Arabs viewed as liberators by many Egyptians because they promised religious tolerance and tax reduction. Egypt became important province of Islamic Empire, beginning over 1300 years of Islamic rule. Ancient Egyptian civilization formally ended, new Arab-Islamic civilization began.

events.title: Establishment of Fustat
events.description: Arab conquerors established Fustat (Old Cairo) on Nile's east bank as Egypt's new capital. Fustat became political, economic and cultural center of Arab Egypt. This city's establishment marked Egypt's entry into Islamic era, Arabic gradually replacing Coptic as main language.

events.title: Umayyad Dynasty Rule
events.description: Egypt became important province under Umayyad Dynasty, providing large amounts of tax revenue and grain to Caliphate. Islam spread in Egypt, but rulers relatively tolerant toward Christians. Arabic language and Islamic culture gradually penetrated, but Coptic Christian community still existed. Egypt's position in Islamic world increasingly important.

events.title: Abbasid Dynasty Rule
events.description: Abbasid Dynasty ruled Egypt after overthrowing Umayyads. Baghdad became new Caliphate capital, Egypt's position relatively declined. But Egypt remained important economic source, Islamization process accelerated. Many Copts converted to Islam, Arabic became dominant language. Egypt gradually lost political autonomy.

events.title: Tulunid Dynasty
events.description: Turkish general Ahmad ibn Tulun established semi-independent Tulunid Dynasty, first independent dynasty in Egypt under Islamic rule. Tulunid Dynasty promoted Egyptian economic development, built many mosques and public facilities. Though nominally still loyal to Abbasid Caliph, actually enjoyed great autonomy.

events.title: Fatimid Conquest
events.description: Shia Fatimid Dynasty conquered Egypt from North Africa, establishing Cairo as new capital. Fatimid Dynasty claimed Caliphate title, opposing Baghdad's Abbasid Dynasty. Cairo became important center of Islamic world, Al-Azhar University established. Under Fatimid rule, Egypt economically prosperous, culture and arts flourished.

events.title: Establishment of Al-Azhar University
events.description: Fatimid Dynasty established Al-Azhar Mosque and University, becoming one of most important academic centers in Islamic world. Al-Azhar University trained countless Islamic scholars, still authoritative institution of Sunni Islam today. This marked Cairo becoming important center of Islamic scholarship and culture.

events.title: Cairo Becomes Capital
events.description: Fatimid Caliph al-Muizz officially transferred capital from Tunisia to newly built Cairo. Cairo (al-Qahira, meaning 'the Victorious') was planned as magnificent royal city with splendid palaces and mosques. Cairo rapidly developed into one of Islamic world's major cultural, economic and political centers, status continuing to present day.

events.title: Saladin Establishes Ayyubid Dynasty
events.description: Kurdish general Saladin overthrew Fatimid Dynasty, established Ayyubid Dynasty, restored Sunni Islamic rule. Saladin unified Egypt and Syria, became hero against Crusaders. He re-established Egypt's leadership position in Islamic world, Cairo became center of resistance against Crusaders.

events.title: Battle of Hattin
events.description: Saladin decisively defeated Crusaders at Battle of Hattin, recaptured Jerusalem. This victory made Saladin hero of Islamic world, Egypt's prestige reached new heights. Saladin's tolerant policies and military talent earned respect from both Muslims and Christians.

events.title: Mamluk Seizure of Power
events.description: Mamluks (slave soldiers) overthrew last Ayyubid Sultan, established Mamluk Sultanate. Mamluks originally Turkish and Caucasian slave soldiers, underwent strict military training. They established unique military aristocratic rule system, ruling Egypt and Syria for nearly 300 years.

events.title: Battle of Ain Jalut
events.description: Mamluk Sultan Baibars I defeated Mongol army at Battle of Ain Jalut, stopping Mongol westward expansion. This was first major defeat of Mongol army in Western Asia, saving Islamic civilization. Egypt became fortress against Mongol invasion, Mamluk prestige greatly increased.

events.title: Mansuri Hospital and School Established
events.description: Mamluk Sultan Qalawun established Mansuri Hospital and School complex in Cairo, becoming one of most advanced medical institutions in medieval Islamic world. Hospital provided free treatment to all patients regardless of religion and social status, with specialized departments and pharmacy. Affiliated medical school trained many physicians, combining ancient Greek medical knowledge with Islamic medical practice.

events.title: Fall of Acre
events.description: Mamluk Sultan Khalil captured Acre, last Crusader stronghold, ending Crusader rule in Levant. This marked complete failure of Crusades, Mamluks became masters of Eastern Mediterranean. Egypt controlled important trade routes from Mediterranean to Red Sea.

events.title: Black Death Pandemic
events.description: Black Death struck Egypt, causing massive population death, estimated mortality rate reached one-third. Plague severely damaged Egyptian economy and social structure, many villages abandoned. This was one of most severe population disasters in Egyptian history, causing long-term impact on Mamluk national strength.

events.title: Burji Mamluk Dynasty
events.description: Burji (Citadel) Mamluks replaced Bahri Mamluks, mainly composed of Circassians. Though this period faced Black Death aftermath and economic difficulties, still maintained military strength, resisting Timur's invasion threat. During Sultans Barsbay and Qaitbay's reigns, Egyptian architectural art reached peak, Cairo's Qaitbay complex became masterpiece of Mamluk architecture.

events.title: Timur's Invasion Threat
events.description: Central Asian conqueror Timur defeated Mamluk army in Syria, captured Damascus and Aleppo. Egypt faced serious threat of conquest, but Timur's death in 1405 spared Egypt. This crisis exposed decline of Mamluk military power, but also prompted Egypt to conduct military reforms.

events.title: Mamluk Golden Age
events.description: Under Mamluk rule, Egypt became important hub of East-West trade, controlling Indian Ocean trade routes. Cairo's population reached 500,000, one of world's largest cities then. Islamic art and architecture reached new heights, many exquisite mosques and mausoleums built. Egypt economically prosperous, culture and arts flourished.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Rounds Cape of Good Hope
events.description: Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama discovered sea route to India, rounding Cape of Good Hope. This discovery broke Egypt's monopoly on East-West trade, Indian Ocean trade began bypassing Egypt. Mamluk economy severely impacted, national strength began declining.

events.title: Battles of Marj Dabiq and Ridaniya
events.description: Ottoman army first defeated Mamluk forces at Battle of Marj Dabiq, then decisively defeated Mamluks at Battle of Ridaniya. Ottoman firearms and modern tactics prevailed against Mamluk cavalry, demonstrating importance of military technological innovation. Last Mamluk Sultan Tuman Bay executed in Cairo, marking end of Mamluk era.

events.title: Ottoman Conquest
events.description: Ottoman Sultan Selim I conquered Egypt, Mamluk Sultanate destroyed. Egypt became Ottoman province, losing political independence. Ottomans retained some Mamluk nobles as local rulers. Cairo's status declined, Istanbul became new political center.

events.title: Venetian Trade Agreement
events.description: Ottoman Egypt signed important trade agreement with Venetian Republic, restoring Mediterranean trade connections. Despite Portuguese opening Cape route, Egypt remained important transit point for East-West trade. Cairo and Alexandria continued attracting European merchants, coffee trade became new economic pillar.

events.title: Ali Bey al-Kabir's Rule
events.description: Mamluk leader Ali Bey al-Kabir effectively broke away from Ottoman control, establishing semi-independent regime. He reformed tax system, developed trade, even conquered Hejaz and parts of Syria. Ali Bey attempted to restore Egypt's independent status, though ultimately failed, laying foundation for later Muhammad Ali's independence movement.

events.title: Battle of the Nile
events.description: British Admiral Nelson destroyed French fleet at Aboukir Bay, also known as Battle of Aboukir Bay. France lost 11 ships of the line, cutting off French forces in Egypt from mainland France. This catastrophic defeat severely weakened Napoleon's position in Egypt, marked establishment of British naval supremacy, ultimately leading to failure of French Egyptian expedition.

events.title: Napoleon's Egyptian Campaign
events.description: Napoleon led French army to Egypt, defeated Mamluk army at Battle of Pyramids. Though French occupation brief (1798-1801), it brought modern science technology and Enlightenment ideas. Napoleon's scholar team conducted comprehensive study of Egypt, discovered Rosetta Stone, opening Egyptology research.

events.title: Discovery of Rosetta Stone
events.description: French officer Pierre-François Bouchard discovered famous Rosetta Stone in town of Rosetta in Nile Delta. This stone inscribed same text in three versions: ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script, and ancient Greek. Rosetta Stone became key to deciphering ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs, French scholar Champollion successfully decoded it in 1822, opening modern Egyptology research.

events.title: French Withdrawal from Egypt
events.description: Under pressure from British-Ottoman coalition, French forces finally withdrew from Egypt, ending three years of occupation. Though militarily defeated, French expedition brought profound impact: publication of Description de l'Égypte introduced Egyptian civilization to Europe, sparked European interest in Egypt. This expedition also broke Egypt's isolation, paving way for later modernization reforms.

events.title: Muhammad Ali Rises to Power
events.description: Albanian officer Muhammad Ali became Egyptian Governor, began modernization reforms. He built modern army, developed industry and agriculture, promoted educational reform. Muhammad Ali called 'Father of Modern Egypt,' his reforms made Egypt one of strongest countries in Middle East.

events.title: Massacre of Mamluks
events.description: Muhammad Ali invited about 500 Mamluk nobles to feast in Cairo Citadel, then killed them, completely eliminating this ruling class. This event called Mamluk Massacre, marked end of old system and beginning of new era. Muhammad Ali thus consolidated absolute rule over Egypt.

events.title: Conquest of Sudan
events.description: Muhammad Ali sent troops to conquer Sudan, controlling upper Nile and gold trade. Sudan became Egyptian colony, providing Egypt with slaves, gold and ivory. This conquest expanded Egyptian territory, strengthened Muhammad Ali's power.

events.title: First Egyptian-Ottoman War
events.description: Muhammad Ali conflicted with Ottoman Sultan, Egyptian army achieved victories in Syria and Anatolia. Egyptian army once approached Istanbul, forcing Sultan to seek Russian help. War result was Egypt gained rule over Syria, greatly increased power.

events.title: Second Egyptian-Ottoman War
events.description: Muhammad Ali again warred with Ottoman Sultan, but this time faced European powers' intervention. Britain, Russia, Austria and Prussia formed alliance supporting Ottomans. Eventually Egypt forced to abandon Syria, but gained hereditary rule over Egypt and Sudan.

events.title: Suez Canal Construction
events.description: French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps supervised Suez Canal construction, taking 10 years to complete. Canal connected Mediterranean and Red Sea, greatly shortening Europe-Asia route. Though bringing income to Egypt, huge construction costs increased Egyptian debt burden, laying groundwork for later financial crisis.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.description: Suez Canal officially opened, European royalty and dignitaries attended opening ceremony. Canal opening made Egypt important hub connecting Europe and Asia, but also attracted greater attention from powers. Canal income became important Egyptian financial source, but control gradually fell into foreign hands.

events.title: Britain Purchases Suez Canal Shares
events.description: Due to financial difficulties, Egyptian Khedive Ismail forced to sell 44% of Suez Canal shares to Britain. British Prime Minister Disraeli quickly decided to purchase, giving Britain canal control. This marked decisive strengthening of British influence over Egypt, laying foundation for later occupation.

events.title: Ismail Deposed
events.description: Due to debt crisis and European powers' pressure, Ottoman Sultan deposed Egyptian Khedive Ismail, succeeded by his son Tawfiq. European creditors controlled Egyptian finances, Egypt actually lost financial sovereignty. This caused strong dissatisfaction among Egyptian nationalists.

events.title: Urabi Revolt
events.description: Egyptian officer Ahmed Urabi led nationalist uprising against foreign control and Khedive's autocratic rule. Uprising gained widespread support, demanding constitution and national independence. Urabi government briefly controlled Egypt, but eventually suppressed by British military intervention.

events.title: British Occupation of Egypt
events.description: British army defeated Urabi army at Battle of Tel el-Kebir, occupied Egypt. Though nominally Egypt remained Ottoman province, actually became British protectorate. British Consul-General became Egypt's actual ruler, beginning 72 years of British rule.

events.title: Mahdist Uprising
events.description: Sudan erupted in Mahdist uprising against Egyptian-British rule. Mahdi Muhammad Ahmad claimed to be Islamic savior, established theocratic state. Uprising army defeated Egyptian forces, captured Khartoum in 1885, British General Gordon killed. Sudan broke away from Egyptian control.

events.title: Suez Canal Convention
events.description: Convention of Constantinople declared Suez Canal as international neutral waterway, allowing free passage for merchant and military vessels of all nations in peace or war. This convention established canal's international legal status, but Britain actually continued controlling canal through occupation of Egypt. Convention terms sparked multiple international disputes in 20th century, culminating in 1956 Suez Crisis.

events.title: Accession of Abbas II
events.description: 18-year-old Abbas Hilmi II succeeded as Egyptian Khedive. He attempted to challenge British control, supported nationalist movement, frequently clashed with British Consul-General Cromer. Abbas II's anti-British stance inspired Egyptian nationalists, but his power always strictly limited by Britain. His reign lasted until deposed in 1914 when Britain formally established protectorate.

events.title: Reconquest of Sudan
events.description: British-Egyptian forces under General Kitchener reconquered Sudan, defeated Mahdist army at Battle of Omdurman. Sudan became Anglo-Egyptian condominium, actually controlled by Britain. This conquest used modern weapons, demonstrating industrial army's overwhelming advantage over traditional forces.

events.title: First Aswan Dam Completed
events.description: Britain completed first modern dam at Aswan to control Nile floods and irrigate farmland. This dam stood 54 meters high, one of world's largest dams at the time. Dam construction transformed Egyptian agricultural production patterns, but also raised controversies about Nile water resource control. This was important milestone in Egypt's modern infrastructure development.

events.title: Entente Cordiale
events.description: Britain and France signed Entente Cordiale, confirming British dominant position in Egypt, in exchange France gained freedom of action in Morocco. This agreement ended long-term rivalry between two countries over Egypt, France abandoned influence in Egypt. Agreement consolidated British control over Egypt, also laid foundation for Anglo-French alliance during World War I.

events.title: Dinshaway Incident
events.description: British officers hunting in Dinshaway village clashed with villagers, resulting in officer's death. British authorities severely retaliated, executing four villagers, causing nationwide Egyptian anger. This incident sparked Egyptian nationalist sentiment, becoming catalyst for anti-British movement.

events.title: National Party Founded
events.description: Mustafa Kamil founded National Party, becoming one of Egypt's earliest modern political parties. National Party advocated complete independence, opposing both British occupation and Ottoman suzerainty. Party spread nationalist ideas through newspaper Al-Liwa, profoundly influencing Egyptian intellectuals and students, advancing anti-British national movement.

events.title: British Protectorate Formally Established
events.description: After World War I outbreak, Britain formally declared Egypt a protectorate, ending nominal Ottoman suzerainty. Khedive deposed, Sultan installed instead. Egypt forced to participate in war, providing base and supplies for British forces. War increased Egyptian people's burden, intensifying national contradictions.

events.title: 1919 Revolution
events.description: After Saad Zaghloul's Wafd Party request to participate in Paris Peace Conference was refused, Egypt erupted in nationwide uprising. Demonstrations, strikes and riots swept the country, Britain forced to use military suppression. Though revolution suppressed, it forced Britain to reconsider Egypt policy, laying foundation for later independence negotiations.

events.title: Egyptian Independence
events.description: Britain unilaterally declared end of protectorate, recognized Egyptian independence, Fuad I became King of Egypt. But Britain reserved four rights: Suez Canal defense, foreign protection, Sudan question and Egyptian defense. This was limited independence, Britain still controlled Egypt's key affairs.

events.title: 1923 Constitution
events.description: Egypt promulgated 1923 Constitution, establishing constitutional monarchy. Constitution stipulated parliamentary government, guaranteed basic rights. Wafd Party won elections, Saad Zaghloul became Prime Minister. But King and Britain maintained important influence, political struggle intense.

events.title: Assassination of Sir Lee Stack
events.description: British Commander-in-Chief in Egypt Sir Lee Stack was assassinated in Cairo. Britain used this as pretext to pressure Egyptian government, demanding suppression of nationalist movement and withdrawal of Egyptian troops from Sudan. This incident caused sharp deterioration in Anglo-Egyptian relations, Wafd Party government forced to resign, Britain strengthened control over Egypt.

events.title: Muslim Brotherhood Founded
events.description: Hassan al-Banna founded Muslim Brotherhood in Ismailia, advocating Islamic revival and social reform. Brotherhood rapidly developed, becoming largest Islamic organization in Middle East. It engaged in both charitable educational work and political activities, profoundly influencing Egypt and entire Islamic world.

events.title: 1930 Constitutional Crisis
events.description: King Fuad I abolished democratic 1923 Constitution, promulgated more authoritarian 1930 Constitution limiting parliamentary powers. This move caused strong opposition from Wafd Party and nationalists. Constitutional crisis intensified triangular struggle between King, Britain and nationalists, Egyptian politics fell into turmoil. 1923 Constitution restored in 1935 under popular pressure.

events.title: Anglo-Egyptian Treaty
events.description: Egypt signed Anglo-Egyptian Treaty with Britain, Britain recognized Egypt's complete independence but retained Suez Canal Zone garrison rights. Egypt joined League of Nations, gained international recognition. Though treaty limited British privileges, still allowed British troops stationed, causing nationalist dissatisfaction.

events.title: Abdeen Palace Incident
events.description: During World War II, British Ambassador surrounded by tanks forced King Farouk to appoint pro-British Wafd Party leader Nahas as Prime Minister. This incident severely damaged reputation of both King and Wafd Party, exposing falsity of Egyptian sovereignty. Incident sparked nationalist sentiment among young officers, becoming important catalyst for 1952 Revolution.

events.title: Formation of Arab League
events.description: Egypt hosted Arab states conference in Cairo, seven Arab countries signed Arab League Charter. Egypt became founding member and headquarters location of Arab League. This marked establishment of Egypt's leadership position in Arab world, Cairo became center of Arab nationalist movement.

events.title: Anti-British Demonstration Movement
events.description: After World War II ended, Egypt erupted in large-scale anti-British demonstration movement demanding British troop withdrawal from Egypt and Sudan. Students and workers held strikes and boycotts, 'Evacuation Day' movement swept the nation. Britain forced to negotiate with Egypt on troop withdrawal, but negotiations progressed slowly, popular discontent remained high.

events.title: First Arab-Israeli War
events.description: After Israel's establishment, Egypt participated in Arab coalition attacking Israel, but suffered defeat. War exposed Egyptian army's corruption and incompetence, causing officers' dissatisfaction. Young officer Nasser and others began plotting to overthrow monarchy, this defeat became important catalyst for 1952 Revolution.

events.title: Free Officers Revolution
events.description: Free Officers organization led by Nasser launched coup, overthrew King Farouk. Revolution almost bloodless, King forced to abdicate and go into exile. Revolutionary Command Council took power, began land reform and social transformation. This marked beginning of modern Egyptian Republic.

events.title: Cairo Fire (Black Saturday)
events.description: Downtown Cairo erupted in massive arson and riots, hundreds of buildings burned including many foreign businesses, hotels, cinemas and nightclubs. This event triggered by British forces killing Egyptian police in Suez Canal Zone, sparking public anger. Fire caused enormous economic losses, severely weakened Farouk dynasty's ruling foundation. This event viewed as prelude to July 1952 Revolution, marking monarchy's collapse had become inevitable.

events.title: Republic Established
events.description: Egypt formally abolished monarchy, declared establishment of republic. Muhammad Naguib became first President, but real power held by Nasser. New government promoted Arab socialist policies, conducted land reform, nationalized important industries.

events.title: Nasser Takes Power
events.description: Nasser defeated Naguib in power struggle, became Egypt's actual leader. He promoted Arab nationalism and socialist policies, became leader of Arab world. Nasser's charisma and ideology influenced entire Middle East region.

events.title: Suez War
events.description: Britain, France and Israel jointly attacked Egypt, attempting to regain Suez Canal control. But under US-Soviet pressure, three countries forced to withdraw. Though Egypt militarily defeated, politically victorious, Nasser became Arab hero. This marked end of British-French influence in Middle East.

events.title: Suez Canal Nationalization
events.description: Nasser announced Suez Canal nationalization, reclaiming canal control. This decision caused strong opposition from Britain, France and Israel, leading to Suez Crisis. Nasser's move viewed as anti-imperialist symbol, greatly enhancing his prestige in Arab world.

events.title: United Arab Republic Established
events.description: Egypt and Syria merged to form United Arab Republic, Nasser as President. This was climax of Arab unity movement, embodying Pan-Arab ideals. But due to political differences and Syrian dissatisfaction, union dissolved in 1961.

events.title: Six-Day War
events.description: Israel launched preemptive attack, defeated Egyptian, Jordanian and Syrian coalition in six days. Egypt lost Sinai Peninsula and Gaza Strip, air force almost completely destroyed. This was major setback for Arab world, Nasser's prestige damaged, forced to conduct military reforms.

events.title: Sadat Succeeds as President
events.description: Anwar Sadat succeeded as Egyptian President, began changing Nasser's policies. Sadat gradually distanced from Soviet Union, turned toward West, promoted economic liberalization policies. His ruling style completely different from Nasser, more pragmatic and flexible.

events.title: Nasser's Death
events.description: Nasser suddenly died of heart attack, aged 52. His funeral attracted millions of mourners, showing his enormous influence in Arab world. Nasser viewed as symbol of Arab nationalism, his death marked end of an era.

events.title: October War (Yom Kippur War)
events.description: Egypt and Syria launched surprise attack on Jewish Yom Kippur, attempting to reclaim lost territories. Egyptian army successfully crossed Suez Canal, broke through Bar Lev Line. Though ultimately not completely militarily victorious, restored Arab army dignity, creating conditions for later peace talks.

events.title: Sadat Visits Jerusalem
events.description: Sadat became first Arab state leader to visit Israel, addressed Israeli Knesset. This historic visit shocked world, opened Egyptian-Israeli peace process. Sadat's brave move brought hope for Middle East peace, but caused strong criticism from Arab world.

events.title: Camp David Accords
events.description: Under US President Carter's mediation, Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Begin signed peace agreement framework at Camp David. Agreement laid foundation for Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty, but Palestinian issue remained unresolved. Sadat and Begin received Nobel Peace Prize for this.

events.title: Egyptian-Israeli Peace Treaty
events.description: Egypt and Israel signed formal peace treaty in Washington, ending 30 years of war between two countries. Israel returned Sinai Peninsula, Egypt recognized Israel. This was first peace treaty between Arab country and Israel, but led to Egypt's expulsion from Arab League.

events.title: Mubarak's Rule
events.description: Hosni Mubarak ruled Egypt for 30 years, maintaining political stability but implementing authoritarian rule. He continued Sadat's pro-Western policies, receiving large US aid. But economic problems, corruption and political repression caused public dissatisfaction. Mubarak became one of longest-serving leaders in Arab world.

events.title: Sadat Assassinated
events.description: Sadat assassinated by Islamic extremists while watching military parade in Cairo. Assassins opposed Sadat's peace policies and secularization reforms. Sadat's death shocked world, but Egyptian-Israeli peace process continued. Vice President Mubarak succeeded as President.

events.title: Gulf War Participation
events.description: Egypt participated in US-led coalition against Iraq's invasion of Kuwait. Egypt sent troops to war, supporting UN resolutions. In return, US forgave most of Egypt's debt, Egypt regained acceptance in Arab world.

events.title: Luxor Terrorist Attack
events.description: Islamic extremists attacked foreign tourists at Hatshepsut Temple in Luxor, killing 62 people. This attack severely damaged Egyptian tourism industry, government strengthened anti-terrorism measures. Event exposed threat of Islamic extremism in Egypt.

events.title: Mubarak Steps Down
events.description: After 18 days of continuous protests, Mubarak announced resignation, ending 30 years of rule. Military took over power, promised democratic transition. Mubarak's fall shocked Arab world, inspired protest movements in other countries.

events.title: January 25 Revolution Begins
events.description: Inspired by Tunisia's Jasmine Revolution, Egyptian people held large-scale protests in Cairo's Tahrir Square and elsewhere, demanding Mubarak's resignation. Demonstrations quickly spread nationwide, millions participated. This marked beginning of Arab Spring in Egypt.

events.title: Morsi Elected President
events.description: Muslim Brotherhood candidate Mohamed Morsi won presidential election, became Egypt's first democratically elected President. This marked political victory for Islamists in Egypt, but also intensified social divisions. Morsi promised to establish inclusive government.

events.title: Military Coup
events.description: After large-scale anti-government demonstrations, military leader Sisi launched coup, overthrew Morsi government. Military claimed this responded to people's will, but Muslim Brotherhood condemned as illegal coup. Egypt fell into political turmoil again.

events.title: Rabaa Massacre
events.description: Security forces violently cleared pro-Morsi sit-in protest camps, causing hundreds of deaths. This was one of bloodiest events in modern Egyptian history, drawing strong international condemnation. After event, Muslim Brotherhood designated as terrorist organization.

events.title: Sisi Elected President
events.description: Former military leader Abdel Fattah el-Sisi won presidential election, officially became Egyptian President. Sisi promised to restore stability and economic development, but critics accused him of establishing new authoritarian rule.

events.title: New Administrative Capital Plan
events.description: Egypt announced grand plan to build new administrative capital east of Cairo, estimated cost $45 billion. New capital will accommodate 5 million people, including government institutions, business districts and residential areas. This is one of largest construction projects in Egyptian history.

events.title: New Suez Canal Opens
events.description: Egypt completed Suez Canal expansion project, new waterway officially opened. Expansion greatly increased canal's transit capacity, reduced transit time. This was important achievement of Sisi government, aimed at increasing canal revenue and enhancing Egypt's strategic position.

events.title: Coptic Church Bombings
events.description: ISIS attacked two Coptic churches before Easter, killing 45 people. This was serious terrorist attack against Egyptian Christians, drawing international attention. Government declared state of emergency, strengthened protection of religious sites.

events.title: Constitutional Amendments
events.description: Egypt passed constitutional amendments extending presidential term to 6 years, allowing Sisi to serve until 2030. Amendments also expanded military powers, drawing criticism from human rights organizations. Supporters said this favored political stability, opponents believed it consolidated authoritarian rule.

events.title: Suez Canal Blockage
events.description: Giant cargo ship Ever Given ran aground in Suez Canal, completely blocking waterway for six days. Event affected global trade, causing billions of dollars in daily losses. After Egypt successfully rescued ship, it highlighted Suez Canal's importance to global economy.

events.title: Pharaohs' Golden Parade
events.description: Egypt held grand Pharaohs' Golden Parade, transferring 22 ancient pharaohs and queens' mummies from Egyptian Museum to new National Museum of Egyptian Civilization. This magnificent ceremony showcased Egypt's rich ancient civilization heritage to world, attracting global attention.

events.title: Economic Crisis and Currency Devaluation
events.description: Egypt faced severe economic crisis, inflation soared, Egyptian pound significantly devalued. Government forced to seek IMF assistance, implement economic reform measures. Crisis affected people's living standards, causing social dissatisfaction.

events.title: New Administrative Capital Partially Operational
events.description: Some government institutions in Egypt's New Administrative Capital began operations, Presidential Palace and some ministries moved in. Though construction continues, new capital already began functioning. This marked important milestone in Egypt's modernization construction.

events.title: Modern Egypt's Challenges and Opportunities
events.description: Egypt under President Sisi strives to balance stability and development. Country faces challenges of population growth, economic difficulties, regional conflicts, but also has advantages of rich historical cultural resources, strategic geographical position and young population. Egypt promoting large infrastructure projects, developing tourism and renewable energy, working toward economic diversification. As largest Arab country, Egypt still plays important role in regional affairs, committed to maintaining Middle East stability and peace.
